Relative clauses are clauses that start with who, that, which, whose, where or when.

You use relative clauses to:
join two separate clauses into one sentence.
Example:
Can I have the report that you showed me this morning?

Give more information about something.
Example:
This is the place where I met my wife.

A defining relative clause gives information about a noun. You need this information to know which noun we are talking about.
A defining relative clause can either be used as subject or object.
When the relative pronoun is the subject, the relative clause can come after the subject or the object of the sentence. You can't drop the relative pronoun.
Example:
The outcome of a bungee jump that nearly resulted in a fatal accident has raised questions about the safety of the sport.
The athlete who attempted the jump was severely injured.

When the relative pronoun is the object, we can drop the relative pronoun if we want to. The clause can come after the subject or the object of the sentence. Example:
The stunt (that) people witnessed was extremely dangerous.
Journalists spoke with other athletes (who) Gina was training with.

A non–defining relative clause gives us extra information about a noun. You don't need this information to know which noun we are talking about.
A non–defining relative clause can either be used as subject or object.
You can't drop the relative pronoun in this kind of clause. You cannot use that in a non-defining relative clause, but always which for an object and who for a person.
A non–defining relative clause can come after the subject.
Example:
Gina, who is an expert jumper, had been preparing for weeks before the jumps.
The stunt that the amused audience witnessed was actually extremely dangerous.
Paddy MacMillan, who was the producer of the half-time show, said he did not understand what had gone wrong.

A non–defining relative clauses can come after the object.
Example:
Experts had expressed concern about the jump, which is one of the hardest stunts to perform.
An adverbial clause is a group of words which have the same function as an adverb. Like all clauses, an adverbial clause has a subject and a verb.

Adverbial clauses of cause are used to express how something happens. An adverb of cause often starts with a subordinating conjunction like as, because, given or since ... to introduce the adverbial clause.

Example:
Organizers didn't know how to prevent the accident, given the short time it took for Gina to perform her jump.
Since Gina was a celebrated world-class jumper, the organizers thought everything would go according to plan.
Because most of the people in the stands didn't realize anything was wrong, they even gave the performers a standing ovation at the end.
As a true performer, Gina continued to act naturally throughout the exhausting experience.

images.text:
The alarming outcome of a bungee jump that nearly resulted in a fatal accident has raised questions about the risky nature of the sport.
</br>
Gina Foster, who is an expert jumper, was performing for the half-time show of the football game when she was caught hanging upside down from her bungee cord. Gina was supposed to do a jump in the middle of the act and then join the other acrobats on the floor.

Instead, after leaping from the tower, Gina was left in a distressing situation. She was dangling from the cord, attached by her left foot, for almost 15 minutes. The stunt that the amused audience witnessed was actually extremely dangerous.
</br>
Journalists spoke with other performers who Gina was training with. They were perplexed and did not know whether it was a change in the program or a malfunction of the bungee apparatus.
</br>
Experts had expressed concern about the jump, which is one of the hardest stunts to perform.
In fact, critics said the accident was almost inevitable, given the short time it took for Gina to prepare for her jump.

Paddy MacMillan, who was the producer of the half-time show, said he did not understand what had gone wrong. Since Gina is a celebrated world-class jumper, she thought everything would go according to plan. Despite the mishap, she was surprised by how well the audience responded. Because most of the people in the stands didn't realize anything was wrong, they even gave the performers a standing ovation at the end.
</br>
MacMillan believes that most of the credit should go to the woman who executed the jump. As a true performer, Gina continued to act naturally throughout the exhausting experience, all the time knowing that the cord could break and send her falling to the floor.
